Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) is a colorless gas with a characteristic rotten egg smell. It's known to be highly flammable and forms explosive mixtures with air. The flammability range is approximately 4.3-46% by volume in air. It has an auto-ignition temperature of about 260°C (500°F).

Ammonium sulfide ((NH₄)₂S) is a salt that can decompose to release hydrogen sulfide and ammonia. While it can be hazardous, it's not typically classified as highly flammable itself.

Cadmium sulfide (CdS) is a solid inorganic compound used in photovoltaic cells and as a pigment. It's not flammable under normal conditions.

Sodium sulfide (Na₂S) is a water-soluble salt that can react with acids to release hydrogen sulfide gas, but the compound itself is not highly flammable.

Among these four inorganic sulfides, hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) is the only one that is highly flammable. It's a gas at room temperature and can easily ignite in the presence of an ignition source when mixed with air at the right concentrations.
